hints: Focus on the standard electrode potentials for the two halogen systems, as the more positive $E^\ominus$ tells you the stronger oxidising agent.
Recall that $E^\ominus$ for $\text{Cl}_2/\text{Cl}^-$ is +1.36 V while $E^\ominus$ for $\text{Br}_2/\text{Br}^-$ is +1.07 V, so chlorine is the stronger oxidiser.
Remember that a stronger oxidising agent takes electrons from the reduced form of the weaker system, turning $\text{Br}^-$ into $\text{Br}_2$.
walkthrough:
**Recall the relevant half-equations and $E^\ominus$ values**

Think of each halogen as an oxidising agent that gains electrons. The bigger the $E^\ominus$, the stronger the oxidiser.

$$\text{Cl}_2 + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Cl}^- \quad E^\ominus = +1.36\,\text{V}$$
$$\text{Br}_2 + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Br}^- \quad E^\ominus = +1.07\,\text{V}$$

**Decide which direction is feasible**

Since $\text{Cl}_2$ has the more positive $E^\ominus$, it will be reduced and will force the other system to be oxidised. That means $\text{Br}^-$ loses electrons.

$$\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{Br}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}^- + \text{Br}_2 \quad E^\ominus_{cell} = +0.29\,\text{V}$$

**Translate into oxidise and reduce language**

Oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain of electrons. Here $\text{Cl}_2$ gains electrons so it is reduced, but it causes $\text{Br}^-$ to lose electrons, so $\text{Cl}_2$ oxidises $\text{Br}^-$. The reverse reaction with $\text{Cl}^-$ and $\text{Br}_2$ would have negative $E^\ominus_{cell}$ and does not occur under standard conditions.

options.A: Correct. $\text{Cl}_2$ is the stronger oxidising agent because its $E^\ominus$ is more positive. It is reduced to $\text{Cl}^-$ while it removes electrons from $\text{Br}^-$, oxidising $\text{Br}^-$ to $\text{Br}_2$. $E^\ominus_{cell}$ is positive (+0.29 V), so this is feasible.
options.B: Incorrect. To reduce $\text{Br}^-$ would mean giving electrons to $\text{Br}^-$, but $\text{Br}^-$ is already fully reduced and cannot gain more electrons. Students choosing this confuse the terms oxidise and reduce.
options.C: Incorrect. $\text{Cl}^-$ is the weaker reducing agent and $\text{Br}_2$ is the weaker oxidising agent in this pair. $\text{Cl}^-$ cannot force electrons onto $\text{Br}_2$ in reverse, and $\text{Cl}^-$ cannot act as an oxidiser because it is already reduced.
options.D: Incorrect. Although $\text{Cl}^-$ acting as a reducer (electron donor) sounds plausible, the $E^\ominus$ values show the reaction $2\text{Cl}^- + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{Br}^-$ has $E^\ominus_{cell} = -0.29$ V and is not feasible under standard conditions. This is the common trap of reversing the spontaneous halogen displacement.
